'''''Eucalyptus leucoxylon''''', commonly known as '''yellow gum''', '''blue gum''' or '''white ironbark''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus leucoxylon'' subsp. ''leucoxylon'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_leucoxylon_subsp._leucoxylon.htm|publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=1 June 2020}}</ref> is a species of small to medium-sized tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to south-eastern continental [[Australia]]. It has smooth yellowish bark with some rough bark near the base, lance-shaped or curved adult leaves, flower buds in groups of three and cylindrical, barrel-shaped or shortened spherical fruit. A widely cultivated species, it has white, red or pink flowers.[[File:Eucalyptus leucoxylon buds.jpg|thumb|right|Flowers and buds]][[File:Eucalyptus leucoxylon fruit.jpg|thumb|right|Fruit]]

==Description==
''Eucalyptus leucoxylon'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|10-30|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has smooth white, yellow or bluish-grey bark, usually with {{cvt|0.5-2|m}} of rough fibrous to flaky bark the base of the trunk. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have leaves mostly arranged in opposite pairs, egg-shaped to broadly lance-shaped, {{cvt|45-105|mm}} long and {{cvt|20-73|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, the same slightly glossy shade of green on both sides, lance-shaped to curved, {{cvt|60-185|mm}} long and {{cvt|10-30|mm}} wide, tapering to a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|9-25|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in groups of three in leaf axils on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|4-11|mm}} long, the individual buds on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|2-14|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval to diamond-shaped or more or less spherical, {{cvt|6-17|mm}} long, {{cvt|5-7|mm}} wide with a conical to rounded or beaked [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering has been recorded in most months and the flowers a white, red or pink. The fruit is a woody, cylindrical, barrel-shaped or shortened spherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|6-13|mm}} long, {{cvt|6-14|mm}} wide with the valves enclosed below rim level.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus leucoxylon'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20leucoxylon |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=14 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian H. |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew V. |title=''Eucalyptus leucoxylon'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/2d91bdc1-4243-4949-bb55-aa26cb06fa7d |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Victoria |access-date=14 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="efloraSA">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus leucoxylon'' |url=http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/speciesfacts_display.cgi?form=speciesfacts&name=Eucalyptus_leucoxylon |publisher=State Herbarium of South Australia |access-date=14 September 2019 |archive-date=26 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210326155333/http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/speciesfacts_display.cgi?form=speciesfacts&name=Eucalyptus_leucoxylon |url-status=dead }}</ref>

This species is similar to ''[[Eucalyptus melliodora|E. melliodora]]'' and [[Eucalyptus sideroxylon|''E. sideroxylon'' subsp. ''sideroxylon'']] but differs in having three buds in each group of flowers.<ref name="ABRS" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus leucoxylon'' was first formally described in 1855 by [[Ferdinand von Mueller]] in the ''Transactions and Proceedings of the Victorian Institute for the Advancement of Science<ref name="F.Muell.">{{cite journal |last1=von Mueller |first1=Ferdinand |title=Description of fifty new Australian plants, chiefly from the colony of Victoria |journal=Transactions and Proceedings of the Victorian Institute for the Advancement of Science |date=1855 |volume=1 |pages=33–34 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/148456#page/47/mode/1up |access-date=14 September 2019}}</ref>''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus leucoxylon''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454873|publisher=APNI|access-date=14 September 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''leucoxylon'') is derived from the [[ancient Greek]] ''leuco-'' meaning "white"<ref name="Stearn">{{cite book |last1=Stearn |first1=William t. |title=Botanical Latin: history, grammar, syntax, terminology, and vocabulary |url=https://archive.org/details/botanicallatin00will |url-access=registration |date=1992 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |isbn=0-88192-321-4 |edition=4th}}</ref>{{rp|441}} and ''-xylon'' meaning "wood".<ref name="Stearn" />{{rp|531}}

==Distribution and habitat==
This eucalypt species is found in Victoria, south-eastern South Australia and far south-western New South Wales. All six subspecies occur in Victoria. Subspecies ''bellarinensis'' is only known from the [[Bellarine Peninsula]] near [[Ocean Grove, Victoria|Ocean Grove]] and [[Torquay, Victoria|Torquay]]. Subspecies ''connata'' grows on skeletal soils, mostly in the [[Brisbane Ranges National Park|Brisbane Ranges]]. Subspecies ''leucoxylon'' is the most widespread species and occurs in scattered populations across Victoria and in south-eastern South Australia, including on [[Kangaroo Island]] where the tallest specimens are found. Subspecies ''megalocarpa'' is a stunted tree or [[Mallee (habit)|mallee]] only found in coastal areas from the far south-east of South Australia to far western Victoria. Subspecies ''pruinosa'' occurs in drier areas of South Australia, the [[Wimmera]] and [[Goldfields region of Victoria|Goldfields]] of Victoria and on the [[Murray River]] floodplain near [[Barham, New South Wales|Barham]]  in New South Wales.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="Rule" /><ref>{{cite book |title=Field Guide to Eucalypts: Volume 1 South Eastern Australia |author1=Brooker. M. I. H. |author2=Kleinig, D. A. |year=2006 |publisher= Bloomings Books |isbn=1-876473-52-5 }}</ref>

==Uses==
===Essential oils===
The leaves are distilled for the production of [[cineole]] based [[eucalyptus oil]].<ref>Boland, D.J., Brophy, J.J., and A.P.N. House, ''Eucalyptus Leaf Oils'', 1991, {{ISBN|0-909605-69-6}}</ref>

===Use in horticulture===
Subspecies ''megalocarpa'' is a relatively small tree with red flowers and large fruit and is often available under the horticultural name 'Rosea'. It flowers profusely in winter, and is widely planted as an [[ornamental plant]].<ref>Brooker, M.I.H. & Kleinig, D.A. ''Field Guide to Eucalyptus'', Bloomings, Melbourne 2001</ref><ref name="ANPSA">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus leucoxylon'' |url=http://anpsa.org.au/e-leu.html |publisher=Australian Native Plants Society, Australia |access-date=14 September 2019}}</ref> 'Euky Dwarf' is grown as a street and garden tree, growing to a height of {{cvt|5-6|m}} tall and {{cvt|3-4|m}} wide.<ref name="Eucalyptus Euky Dwarf">{{Cite web|url=http://austraflora.com/project/eucalyptus-euky-dwarf/|title=Eucalyptus Euky Dwarf|website=Austraflora|date=15 July 2013 |language=en-US|access-date=2016-03-28}}</ref> Subspecies ''leucoxylon'' has been recommended for larger gardens and parklands.<ref>{{cite web|title=South Australian blue gum|url=http://www.stateflora.sa.gov.au/about-us/latest-articles/blue-gum|website=State Flora|access-date=5 March 2016|archive-date=7 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307070841/http://www.stateflora.sa.gov.au/about-us/latest-articles/blue-gum|url-status=dead}}</ref>
